edits.old: that built and ran the 4,000 MW supercritical coal-fired Mundra Ultra Mega Power Project in Gujarat.
edits.new: that built and ran the supercritical coal-fired Mundra Ultra Mega Power Project in Gujarat. The plant's two capacity figures are different quantities, and a regulator's order sets both out: the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, in its order of 20 June 2025 on CGPL's own petition 168/MP/2019, describes the project as having "an installed capacity of 4,150 MW (5x830 MW)", and records CGPL's affidavit that "[t]he net plant capacity is 4000 MW (5 units of 800 MW each) after accounting for the Motor Driven Boiler Feed Pump" and that "[d]espite each unit being rated for 830 MW, the net plant capacity remains 4,000 MW". The Commission's own finding is that expenditure is computed on the 4,150 MW installed capacity but the buyers' liability is limited to 4,000 MW, because the power purchase agreement "is limited to 4000 MW". The 4,000 MW figure is the one the IFC's disclosure uses. The contracted ex-bus output to the procurers is lower again, at 3,800 MW.

edits.old: starting with the 178 MW Shuakhevi and 6 MW Skhalta plants.
edits.new: starting with the Shuakhevi and Skhalta plants. The sizes given for it do not agree, and the disagreement starts inside the IFC's own disclosure for project 33435: its Summary of Investment Information calls the financed project 184 MW and says it consists of the 178 MW Shuakhevi plant and the 6 MW Skhalta plant; its Environmental and Social Review Summary says 184 MW in one place and 185 MW in another; its Early Disclosure of 24 May 2013 says 185 MW. The Asian Development Bank's press release of 19 March 2015 says 187 MW, and ADB's monitoring reports break that down as a 178 MW Shuakhevi plant plus a 9 MW Skhalta plant, labelling the 187 MW a gross figure with the net left to be filled in at commercial operation. The EBRD's environmental study gives the scheme as 185 MW with a 10 MW Skhalta plant. The plant that differs between the accounts is Skhalta, at 6, 9 or 10 MW, and no document says which of 184, 185 and 187 MW the others are.

edits.old: Project company owned by Huaneng Shandong Power Generation (51%) and Shandong Ruyi (49%) (AidData)
edits.new: Project company. Its shareholding is given two ways in documents NEPRA published with its generation licence application. The project's feasibility study, under "Investment mode", says the plant "shall be built in form of joint venture, and each shareholder's shares are as follows: Huaneng Shandong Power Generation Co., Ltd. 51%; Shandong Ruyi Science & Technology Group Co., Ltd. 49%" - the figures AidData repeats, without saying which of its 65 listed sources it took them from. The same bundle's prospectus says that on 22 May 2014 "Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (HK) Energy Limited was incorporated, with Huaneng Shandong Power Generation Co., Ltd. and Ruyi Group holding 50% of the shares respectively", and that on 28 May 2014 the Pakistani company "was incorporated as a wholly owned subsidiary of Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (HK) Energy Limited"; the memorandum of association in the same bundle records the Hong Kong company holding 99,995 of the 100,000 shares. The rating agency PACRA, in July 2022, likewise calls the Pakistani company "a wholly owned subsidiary of Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Hong Kong) Energy Limited". Global Energy Monitor gives the Hong Kong company as 50% Huaneng Shandong Power Generation and 50% Jining Chengtou Holding Group, with Shandong Ruyi absent. NEPRA's tariff decision names no shareholders.

edits.old: Plant owner and borrower; 60% owned by Korea Electric Power Corporation Philippine Holdings and 40% by SPC Power Corporation
edits.new: Plant owner and borrower. The 60/40 split rests on newspaper reporting rather than a filing: the Philippine Star reported on 19 January 2023 that KEPCO was selling "its 60 percent stake in KEPCO SPC Power Corp.", and on 21 October 2007, when the venture was formed, that Salcon Power would "invest 40 percent in the project" with 60 per cent of the project's total capitalisation from Kephilco - figures the article frames as shares of investment and capitalisation. SPC Power Corporation's own annual report on SEC Form 17-A for 2022 states its side of it - "KEPCO SPC Power Corporation (KSPC). KSPC, 40% owned by the Parent Company, was incorporated on June 22, 2005" - but no filing found states KEPCO's 60%. Global Energy Monitor prints a 60/40 the other way round, Salcon Power 60 and KEPCO 40, but that is the ownership of SPC Power Corporation itself in its account of the retired first Naga plant, not of the joint venture.
